lesson.title: jener ↔ yon & the Demonstrative Map
lesson.subtitle: dieser/jener ↔ this/yon — and der/die/das with demonstrative force

hook.title: This, That, and the Word English Lost
hook.content: English once had three distances: this (near me), that (near you), yon (far from both of us). Yonder's parent word — yon — is now poetic at best. German kept the full map: dieser ↔ this, das ↔ that, jener ↔ yon. That makes jener the oldest word in the set — the twin of a word English pushed out to the frontier ('yonder man'). And stressed der/die/das still carry demonstrative force: 'DER Mann da' is 'THAT man there', with the article doing the pointing.

footnotes.title: Yon Is Yonder's Root
footnotes.content: yon, yonder, and jener all descend from the same Proto-Germanic *jēnaz. English kept it only in the far-distance compound yonder; German's jener is the bare survivor — the demonstrative of the horizon.

pattern.title: The Three-Distance Map
pattern.content: Near: dieser Tag (this day) — declension alert: dieser is the ein-family's twin, so masculine accusative gives diesen Tag. Far: jener Mann (yon man) — same endings as dieser, pointing past your conversation partner. The default: der/die/das, which double as 'the' — but under stress they point: DER Mann da (THAT man there). Compare with topic 12's negation grid and you see the system: ein-family (kein, mein) and pointer-family (dieser, jener) decline identically; only der/die/das march to their own ancient beat.
pattern.linguist_note: That's why dieser and jener take the same endings as ein and kein (dieser → diesen) while der → den: German demonstratives come in two ancient lineages, and English 'this/that' descends from both (þis from the same base as German dies-).

exercises.prompt: Match the three distances with their German pointers:
exercises.target_answer: dieser, jener, das, der, jener Baum, dieser Nebel, jene Insel, dieser Teller
exercises.meaning: this, yon, that, the/he, yon tree, this fog, yon island, this plate
exercises.explanation: One map: dieser (near), jener (far) — with der/die/das as the default articles. The new nouns ride the map like everything else.

exercises.prompt: Which English word is the bare twin of 'jener'?
exercises.explanation: yon/yonder and jener share Proto-Germanic *jēnaz. English keeps yon only in 'yonder'; German kept the bare form. Your room words line up on the map too: dieses Bett (this bed — das Bett, neuter), dieses Fenster (this window) — the ein-family endings decide.

exercises.prompt: Accusative alert: 'Ich nehme _____ Löffel' (dieser + masculine object):
exercises.english_hint: dieser declines like ein: dies + en
exercises.meaning: Ich nehme diesen Löffel = I take this spoon
exercises.explanation: dieser copies the ein-family: masculine accusative -en (diesen), exactly like einen and keinen — der Löffel pays the same toll.

exercises.prompt: 'DER Mann da!' — what does the stressed article do here?
options: It points — the article carries demonstrative force: THAT man there
exercises.target_answer: It points — the article carries demonstrative force: THAT man there
exercises.explanation: Under stress, the plain article resumes its ancient demonstrative job — the/that were one word originally.

exercises.prompt: Say in German: "This chair is good"
exercises.explanation: dieser + masculine der Stuhl — near-distance pointing, verb in position 2. The chair passes inspection.
cues: Start with "Dieser" and anchor "Stuhl" in position 2.

summary.outcome: Use dieser and jener across the three-distance map and decline dieser like the ein-family.
summary.takeaway: dieser ↔ this, das ↔ that, jener ↔ yon — and stressed der/die/das point again whenever German needs them to.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: Possessive Ladders — mein, dein, sein, ihr across the grid, with the KJV 'mine/thine' rule.

twist.prompt: Without looking back — rebuild the core sentence from jener ↔ yon & the Demonstrative Map (This chair is good):
twist.explanation: Re-assembling "Dieser Stuhl ist gut" from scratch locks in the structural pattern of jener ↔ yon & the Demonstrative Map without relying on short-term echo.

jener.context_translation: That man over there (yon man) is tall.
jener.etymology_derivation: The far demonstrative — the twin of archaic English yon/yonder (Proto-Germanic *jēnaz). [wiktionary]

dieser.etymology_derivation: North Sea Germanic demonstrative: Old English þis and German dieser are one system — dies- ↔ this. [wiktionary]

die.etymology_derivation: th → d. Sounds identical to emphatic English "thee".

das.shift_rule: TH → D + T → S / SS / Z
das.etymology_derivation: Double shift: th → d and final t → s.

haus.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *hūsą — an exact twin of English house, down to the diphthong. [wiktionary]

tag.etymology_derivation: Double shift: d → t and y → g.

insel.context_translation: The island lies in the south.
insel.etymology_derivation: From Old High German isila, borrowed from Latin insula. English isle and insular come from the same Latin word. [wiktionary]

nebel.context_phrase: Im Herbst gibt es oft Nebel.
nebel.context_translation: In autumn there is often fog.
nebel.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *nebulaz, from PIE *nébʰos — inherited Germanic, PIE-kin to English nebula. [wiktionary]

baum.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *baumaz — English beam is the cognate; a beam was originally a tree. [wiktionary]

bett.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *badją — explicitly cognate with English bed; the High German d→t gives the final -tt. [wiktionary]

teller.etymology_derivation: From Middle French tailloir, meaning cutting board, from the Old French cutting verb tailler; English tailor descends from the same Old French verb. [wiktionary]

stuhl.context_translation: The chair stands at the table.
stuhl.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *stōl — cognate with English stool; the meaning narrowed from stool to chair. [wiktionary]

fenster.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *fenestr, an early borrowing of Latin fenestra — a Latin loan both languages share. [wiktionary]

löffel.context_phrase: Nimm einen Löffel für die Suppe.
löffel.context_translation: Take a spoon for the soup.
löffel.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic lapilaz, from the root lap, meaning to lick or lap; English lap is the related word, and its p appears as f in German. [wiktionary]

th_to_d.name: The Dental Shift (TH → D)
th_to_d.historical_linguistics: Every single original Germanic "th" sound systematically shifted to "d" in High German, while English kept the ancient "th".
th_to_d.philological_note: Around 500–700 AD in the High German Consonant Shift, dental fricatives hardened into voiced dental stops.

d_to_t.name: The Stop Shift (D → T)
d_to_t.historical_linguistics: Where English kept Germanic "d", High German hardened it into "t".
d_to_t.philological_note: Voiced stops became voiceless. Explains pairs like day ↔ Tag, door ↔ Tür, and drink ↔ trinken.
d_to_t.literature_source: Complementary to the TH → D shift: as TH took over D, original D shifted to T in High German.

p_to_pf_f.name: The Labial Shift (P → PF / F)
p_to_pf_f.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /p/ shifted to the affricate "pf" at the beginning of words, and to "f" or "ff" after vowels.
p_to_pf_f.philological_note: Explains apple ↔ Apfel, pepper ↔ Pfeffer, hope ↔ hoffen, and sleep ↔ schlafen.

t_to_s_ss_z.name: The Sibilant Shift (T → S / SS / Z)
t_to_s_ss_z.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /t/ shifted to sibilant "s/ss/ß" after vowels, and to "z" (/ts/) at the beginning of words.
t_to_s_ss_z.philological_note: Reveals water ↔ Wasser, eat ↔ essen, better ↔ besser, two ↔ zwei, and to ↔ zu.
t_to_s_ss_z.literature_source: Walter Skeat - Primary dental affrication and spirantization

k_to_ch.name: The Velar Shift (K → CH)
k_to_ch.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /k/ softened to the fricative "ch" in medial and final positions.
k_to_ch.philological_note: The Ach-Laut [x] occurs after a, o, u; the Ich-Laut [ç] occurs after e, i, ä, ö, ü.

v_to_b.name: The Bilabial Shift (V / F → B)
v_to_b.historical_linguistics: Intervocalic /v/ and /f/ in English regularly correspond to voiced /b/ in German.
v_to_b.philological_note: Explains give ↔ geben, live ↔ leben, love ↔ lieben, over ↔ über, and seven ↔ sieben.
v_to_b.literature_source: Proto-Germanic bilabial spirant closing to stop in High German

y_gh_to_g_ch.name: The Palatal & Guttural Link (Y → G & GH → CH)
y_gh_to_g_ch.historical_linguistics: English vocalized palatal "g" into "y" (say, day, yesterday) and silenced "gh" (night, laugh, light). German preserved them as "g" or "ch".
y_gh_to_g_ch.philological_note: Explains why English spelling has silent 'gh' letters — they were original German-like gutturals!

latin_ieren.name: The Latin / Romance Layer (-ate / -ize → -ieren)
latin_ieren.phonetic_rule: English verbs ending in -ate, -ize, -ify, -ish ➔ German verbs ending in -ieren
latin_ieren.historical_linguistics: English verbs derived from Latin or French directly map to German verbs ending in -ieren.
latin_ieren.philological_note: Past participles of -ieren verbs never take the "ge-" prefix (studieren → studiert).
latin_ieren.literature_source: Middle High German productive loan suffix from Old French -ier

strong_verbs_ablaut.name: The 7 Strong Verb Classes (Ablaut)
strong_verbs_ablaut.phonetic_rule: English irregular strong verbs with internal vowel changes ➔ German strong verbs following the exact same Ablautreihe
strong_verbs_ablaut.historical_linguistics: Shared 7 Proto-Germanic verb classes where tenses are formed by shifting root vowels.
